strengths: Identifies an important and previously underexplored conceptual bottleneck in AR-based generative classification: the restrictive inductive bias imposed by fixed raster-scan token orderings.

The proposed order-marginalized AR generative classification framework is intuitive and elegant, naturally leveraging any-order autoregressive modeling (RandAR) to compute the order-marginalized likelihood bound.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the method sets a new state-of-the-art among generative classifiers on ImageNet-1K and diverse OOD benchmarks (ImageNet-R/S/A/C, WILDS), outperforming diffusion classifiers (DiT, SiT) by large margins while offering up to 25x faster inference.

Insightful analysis of AR classifiers, including spatial per-token discriminative log-likelihood visualizations, prefix length sensitivity, VQ-VAE tokenizer robustness, and noise augmentation ablation.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is relatively modest: the proposed inference procedure directly evaluates the lower bound on order-unconditional log-likelihood using Monte Carlo sampling of random permutations, which directly corresponds to the standard training loss formulation of RandAR.

Like all generative classifiers, classification still scales linearly with the number of classes (requiring M × K forward passes), which remains substantially slower than standard feed-forward discriminative classifiers and necessitates evaluation on subsets (2K images) for 1000-class ImageNet validation.

The DINOv2 baseline was trained from scratch on ImageNet-1K for 200 epochs, which may not represent the strongest possible discriminative SSL baseline compared to standard longer pretraining schedules, although the comparison is nonetheless informative.

strengths: Insightful and timely motivation: While diffusion models have dominated recent literature on generative classification due to their iterative coarse-to-fine nature, this work identifies the restrictive inductive bias of fixed-order generation (e.g., raster scan) as a major impediment for autoregressive (AR) models and provides an effective remedy via any-order AR modeling.

Order-marginalized formulation: Deriving the order-marginalized classifier via the expected log-likelihood lower bound (Eq. 5) is intuitive and well-justified empirically against the direct Monte Carlo likelihood estimate.

Comprehensive empirical benchmarking: The authors evaluate across diverse settings (ImageNet-1K validation, out-of-distribution robustness on ImageNet-R/S/A/C, and subpopulation shifts on WILDS), comparing against state-of-the-art diffusion classifiers (DiT, SiT, REPA), other AR classifiers (LlamaGen, VAR, A-VARC), and strong discriminative baselines (ViT, DINOv2).

Substantial speedup over diffusion classifiers: Evaluating order-marginalized AR requires only one forward pass per order/class (typically K=5 to 20), achieving up to 25x speedup compared to diffusion classifiers requiring 100-250 evaluations while delivering superior accuracy.

Detailed analyses and ablations: The paper includes thoughtful analyses, such as per-token discriminative likelihood visualizations across different K values, token accuracy vs. prefix length, tokenizer robustness to continuous noise perturbations, and token-pruning experiments in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty on the generative modeling side: The method primarily applies an existing any-order AR architecture (RandAR) to classification via multi-order averaging. While the application and findings are novel and valuable for generative classifiers, the architectural contribution itself is modest.

Practical scaling to large class spaces: Although significantly more efficient than diffusion classifiers, generative classification via Bayes' rule still requires conditioning on all target classes (producing [M, K] forward sequences). A brief discussion or analysis of candidate pruning or hierarchical filtering to scale inference to larger class vocabularies would strengthen practical applicability.

Dependence on VQ tokenizer choice and noise augmentation: As shown in Section 6.4, performance is somewhat sensitive to tokenizer codebook size and latent noise perturbation during pretraining, indicating that the discrete representation remains a delicate component in AR generative classification.

strengths: Compelling conceptual insight: The paper makes an astute observation regarding the limitation of fixed-order (e.g., raster scan) visual autoregressive models in generative classification. Framing diffusion models as implicit spectral autoregression and proposing order marginalization via any-order AR models (specifically RandAR) is intuitive and well-motivated.

Strong empirical results: RandAR-based classifiers significantly outperform diffusion classifiers (DiT, SiT) across standard ImageNet and out-of-distribution benchmarks (IN-R, IN-S, IN-C), narrowing the gap to state-of-the-art self-supervised discriminative representations (DINOv2) to just 1.4% on ImageNet-Val while outperforming DINOv2 on several OOD datasets.

Dramatic efficiency gains: AR models evaluate order-conditional log-likelihoods in a single forward pass per order. As a result, order-marginalized AR achieves up to 25x faster inference compared to diffusion classifiers at comparable or superior classification accuracy.

Thorough analysis and ablations: The paper provides rich diagnostic insights, including per-token discriminative likelihood visualizations across different prefix lengths and orders, ablations comparing direct log-likelihood estimation vs. the Jensen lower bound, evaluations across tokenizer codebook sizes, and real-world distribution shifts on WILDS benchmarks.
weaknesses: Incremental methodological novelty: The algorithmic contribution relies almost entirely on deploying an off-the-shelf any-order model (RandAR) and applying Monte Carlo sample averaging over random orders using its standard training objective (the Jensen lower bound). The methodological novelty is relatively light, though the empirical discovery and analysis are strong.

Inherent scalability limitations of generative classifiers: Although AR order-marginalization is much faster than diffusion classifiers, classification still scales linearly with the number of candidate classes $M$ (requiring $M \times K$ forward evaluations), which restricts evaluation to small subsets (2K images) on 1000-class ImageNet benchmarks following prior DC protocols.

Limited theoretical justification for the estimator discrepancy: Section 4 notes that the Jensen lower bound $\mathbb{E}_\pi [\log p(\mathbf{x}|\pi, c)]$ significantly outperforms the direct likelihood estimator $\log \mathbb{E}_\pi [p(\mathbf{x}|\pi, c)]$. While the authors hypothesize this is due to alignment with the training loss, further formal analysis or empirical variance study across different orders is lacking.

Substantial gap on ImageNet-A: While competitive on IN-R and IN-S, RandAR-XL lags noticeably behind DINOv2 on ImageNet-A (0.233 vs. 0.345), indicating that susceptibility to natural adversarial examples remains a challenge for generative models compared to self-supervised discriminative backbones.

strengths: Timely and significant contribution: While diffusion models have dominated visual generative classification, this paper convincingly demonstrates that modern visual autoregressive (AR) models, when relieved of fixed raster-order constraints, can significantly outperform diffusion classifiers.

Sound motivation and insightful analysis: The exploration of order marginalization is backed by compelling visualizations and empirical analyses (e.g., discriminative per-token log-likelihoods, prefix-length accuracy curves, and spatial token heatmaps).

Substantial empirical gains: The proposed approach achieves superior in-domain accuracy (81.3% on ImageNet-Val with RandAR-XL vs. 77.2% for DiT-XL) and demonstrates strong out-of-distribution robustness across ImageNet-R/S/C and WILDS benchmarks, often competing favorably with strong self-supervised baselines like DINOv2.

Dramatic efficiency advantage: By computing full-sequence order-conditional log-likelihoods in single forward passes, the approach achieves up to 25x speedup compared to standard multi-step diffusion classifiers.

Extensive and rigorous experimental validation: The authors thoroughly compare against diverse baselines (supervised ViT, DINOv2, DiT, SiT with REPA, few-step MeanFlow, VAR, LlamaGen, and DAT), perform appropriate ablations (loss weighting, VQ-VAE tokenizers, likelihood formulations), and test across multiple architectures (RandAR and RAR).
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is relatively incremental from a modeling perspective: The framework predominantly adapts existing any-order AR models (RandAR / RAR) by taking a Monte Carlo average of log-likelihoods across sampled permutation orders, rather than introducing a new architectural paradigm.

Inherent computational bottleneck of generative classification: Although much faster than diffusion classifiers, computing p(x|c) still scales linearly with the number of classes M (requiring K passes per class, totaling M x K forward evaluations per image), which limits real-time deployment and necessitated evaluating 2K subsets for 1000-class benchmarks.

strengths: Clear insight and strong motivation: The paper identifies a fundamental limitation of classical visual autoregressive (AR) models for generative classification—the restrictive inductive bias of fixed raster-order generation—and proposes order marginalization using any-order AR models (e.g., RandAR, RAR) to address it.

Substantial empirical gains: The proposed order-marginalized AR classifier substantially outperforms previous generative classifiers (including diffusion models like DiT and SiT, as well as raster-order AR models like LlamaGen and VAR). RandAR-XL reaches 81.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K, closing the gap with strong discriminative models such as DINOv2 and outperforming them on multiple out-of-distribution benchmarks (IN-R, IN-S, IN-C).

High efficiency gain over diffusion classifiers: Evaluating order-conditional log-likelihoods in a single forward pass enables order-marginalized AR classifiers to achieve superior classification accuracy with far fewer evaluations (e.g., K=4 to 20) compared to diffusion classifiers requiring 100-250 steps, translating to an empirical speedup of up to 25x.

Comprehensive empirical analysis and ablation studies: The paper provides informative analyses, including per-token discriminative likelihood visualizations across different K values, token accuracy as a function of prefix length, tokenizer robustness and noise augmentation, comparison between the Jensen lower bound and direct likelihood estimation, and theoretical/empirical comparisons with masked diffusion.
weaknesses: Incremental methodological novelty: The underlying any-order architecture (RandAR) and its training objective are taken directly from prior work. The classification methodology is a straightforward application of Bayes' rule with a Monte Carlo average over random permutations using the model's training lower-bound.

Inference cost remains prohibitive compared to discriminative classifiers: While significantly faster than diffusion classifiers, classifying an image still requires evaluating K forward passes across all candidate classes (e.g., taking tens of seconds per image on an A100 GPU for 1000 classes), which necessitates evaluating on 2K-subsets for ImageNet benchmarks.

Limited exploration of non-uniform or adaptive order sampling: Random permutations are sampled uniformly, yet the paper's own analysis (e.g., Figures 4 and 5) shows that central tokens and intermediate prefix lengths provide vastly different discriminative value. Investigating importance-sampling or heuristic ordering strategies could have further improved sample efficiency.

strengths: Compelling conceptual premise: The paper insightfully identifies a key limitation of prior visual autoregressive (AR) generative classifiers—namely, their rigid raster-scan inductive bias—and effectively demonstrates that order marginalization over any-order AR (AO-AR) models unlocks substantially higher discriminative representation fidelity.

Dramatic efficiency improvement over diffusion classifiers: Generative classification has historically been bottlenecked by extreme inference latency (requiring 100-250 diffusion sampling steps per class). By leveraging parallel token-likelihood computation in AR forward passes, the proposed order-marginalized framework outperforms diffusion classifiers (DiT/SiT) while offering up to 25x speedup.

Extensive and rigorous benchmarking: The empirical validation is thorough, evaluating in-domain ImageNet-1K, diverse out-of-distribution benchmarks (IN-R, IN-S, IN-C, IN-A), real-world distribution/subpopulation shifts on WILDS (CelebA, Camelyon17, FMoW), and complex settings (ObjectNet, COCO). Comparing against both generative models and strong self-supervised discriminative baselines (e.g., DINOv2) sets a high standard for generative classification literature.

Deep technical analysis and ablations: The manuscript provides illuminating analyses, including per-token discriminative log-likelihoods, token accuracy vs. prefix length, mathematical and empirical equivalence/distinction to masked diffusion models, tokenizer codebook robustness, and comparisons against few-step diffusion baselines (MeanFlow).
weaknesses: Modest algorithmic novelty: The core technique essentially applies Monte Carlo averaging of log-likelihoods across random permutation sequences using an existing any-order autoregressive architecture (RandAR / unannealed RAR). While the application and empirical findings are valuable, the algorithmic contribution itself is fairly straightforward.

Inherent scalability bottleneck across class counts: Although significantly faster than diffusion classifiers, generative classification via Bayes' rule still requires evaluating likelihoods across all candidate classes $M$. For large class vocabularies (e.g., 1000 classes in ImageNet) combined with $K=20$ orders, the total number of evaluations per image remains substantial, necessitating evaluation on 2K sub-samples as noted in Section 6.1.

Dependence on specialized training augmentations: The optimal performance of the RandAR classifier relies on pretraining with specific latent noise augmentations and random cropping (Section 6.4), meaning that off-the-shelf generative AR checkpoints cannot necessarily reproduce these results without tailored retraining.

Minor typographical inconsistency in theoretical derivations: In Appendix D, Eq. (6), the conditioning term in line 4 is written as $\mathbf{x}_{\pi(<t)}$ rather than $\mathbf{x}_{\pi(<n)}$, which appears to be an index typo.
